messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amara was twenty-three when the helicopter went down. She had been a military surgeon deployed to a forward operating base, and the MEDEVAC evacuation was routine until the RPG struck the tail rotor. The cabin lurched, then spun, and she remembered the sound—a percussive blast that seemed to slam into her chest before the world turned upside down. She woke pinned under a fuel bladder, the smell of aviation fuel and blood thick in her throat, her face pressed against a torn piece of canvas that had the rough, gritty texture of sand fused with something wet. She couldn't move; she could hear the rotors winding down in a slow, grinding whine that seemed to go on forever. When the rescue team pulled her out, she had no words for what had happened—the sequence of images was a jumble of pressure, noise, and that specific feeling of grit against her cheek, but she could never put it into a straight narrative. It came back whole, or not at all.

That was two years ago. Now Amara works as a trauma surgeon in a civilian hospital in a large city, and she has learned to live with a kind of constant alertness she never needed before. She always sits with her back to the wall in the doctors' lounge, the cafeteria, even in the conference room—she needs to see the door and both windows, needs to know the nearest exit. Before she walks into any room, she maps an escape route: if someone came through that door, she would go left, past the crash cart, out the service corridor. She scans every new environment without meaning to, her eyes flicking to corners, to ceiling tiles, to anyone who moves too quickly. These habits started after the crash, but they have become automatic. It is not that she thinks about the event when she does them; it is that the event has taught her that danger can come from anywhere, without warning.

The triggers are scattered through her day like landmines. A helicopter from the hospital's Life Flight pad sends a thrumming through the walls, and her chest tightens before she can tell herself it's just a medevac, not a crash. A bang from the janitor dropping a metal cart in the hallway makes her flinch, her hand flying to the scalpel in her pocket before she even registers the sound. And then there is the feeling of certain textures: the stiff, blood-soaked gauze she peels off a wound, the way it feels almost crystalline against her gloved fingers—that gritty canvas sensation floods back, and the terror is instantaneous. She cannot talk about it; when a colleague once asked what happened, Amara found she could only shake her head, the images too formless and too vivid at the same time.

The memory itself arrives without warning, too. She will be standing in the OR, steady and focused, and then a sound or a sensation will pull her back into that twisted cabin, and she is there again—the same crushing fear, the same certainty that she is about to die. It is not a memory she recalls; it is a memory that invades. She has come to believe that if she ever stops scanning, stops planning, stops sitting with her back to the wall, another explosion will find her. So she keeps doing it, and the more she scans, the more she notices the helicopter, the more she flinches at bangs, the more she feels the grit in everyday objects. She is not aware that her own vigilance is feeding the triggers; she only knows that the world feels unsafe, and that being prepared is the only thing that seems to help. At work, she has started to avoid the break room near the emergency stairwell because it has no second exit, and she sometimes asks residents to meet her elsewhere. They have noticed her checking the corners, but they attribute it to a surgeon's intensity.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the operating room last week. A patient had been brought in with multiple shrapnel wounds from a construction accident, and as she packed the wound, her gloved hand touched a piece of gravel embedded in the tissue. The texture was wrong—it was the same grit, the same wet sand—and for a full ten seconds she froze, her hand suspended, her heart hammering, the patient open on the table. A nurse called her name twice before she heard it. She finished the surgery, but that night she could not sleep, and she sat against the wall of her apartment, mapping exits until dawn. She is most afraid that next time she will not be able to move at all, that the patient will die because of a piece of gravel. She is hoping that by talking to someone, she can learn to walk into a room without counting the doors.
